newsitem.title: USA: Industry opposes most post-TWA center tank ideas.
newsitem.headline: Industry opposes most post-TWA center tank ideas.

text.p: An international group of airlines and plane manufacturers on Thursday said they opposed nearly all the National Transportation Safety Board's recommendations for center fuel tanks.
NTSB made the proposals to minimize the chances of fuel-air fumes igniting and destroying an aircraft as the board believes happened just over a year ago to TWA Flight 800.
But the industry group said commercial aircraft fuel systems were already highly reliable and any changes could create new risks and required careful study.
The NTSB proposals were issued in December 1996 once it became clear the center tank between the wings and under the passenger deck was the center of the TWA blast.
The ideas ranged from nitrogen inerting of the vapor in the center fuel tank down to filling the tank with a small amount of cool fuel before flight.
But in a submission to the Federal Aviation Administration, which requested comment on the NTSB ideas, the industry group said the existing focus on preventing ignition sources remained correct.
Only the NTSB proposal for insulation of the center tank from heat-generating air-conditioning equipment was given any weight.
"There may be some benefit from minimizing heat transfer from equipment located in the vicinity of fuel tanks," the aircraft users and makers said in their executive summary.
Nitrogen inerting systems were described by the industry group as unreliable and likely to introduce new safety concerns.
Increased aircraft weight from the inerting system would shorten aircraft range, causing more landings and takeoffs -- the most likely time for an accident to occur.

Tanks could rupture and expose passengers and employees to hazardous levels of odorless and colorless nitrogen. The group also said a comprehensive analysis of the cooler fuel idea showed no significant improvement in safety.
Instead, the aviation industry group proposed establishing an international fuel-tank group to inspect the wiring, condition of fuel pumps and the electrical bonding of all commerical aircraft tanks.

"As a long-term action, the industry suggests that the NTSB and FAA consider requesting the petroleum industry to develop aviation fuels that will reduce exposure to flammable air-fuel vapors," the group said.
The NTSB has not completed its investigation of the TWA crash that killed 230 people on July 17, 1996, when the Boeing 747 exploded shortly after leaving New York.
The NTSB is working with research centers around the world to determine exactly what set off the explosion in the nearly empty center tank.

The organizations making the submission to the FAA were the Air Transport Association, the Aerospace Industries Association, the Association of European Aerospace Industries, the Association of European Airlines and the Association of Asia Pacific Airlines.
